sections.label: Section A - Reading Skills, General Knowledge & Logical Reasoning

questions.stem:
"Take this medicine at evenly spaced times as prescribed and complete the full course, even if your symptoms improve, because stopping early can let the infection return. If you forget a dose, take it as soon as you remember, but skip the missed dose if your next dose is due soon; never take a double dose. Return any unused tablets to a pharmacy: they must not be kept to treat future illnesses or given to other people."

From the informational leaflet for an antibiotic

Which of the following statements is the correct interpretation of the instructions?
options: Stopping the course when symptoms improve is the recommended way to avoid side effects.
Two tablets should be taken together whenever a dose is missed.
Leftover tablets must not be saved to treat a later illness.
This antibiotic should always be taken with food.
Sharing the medicine with a family member who has similar symptoms is acceptable.
questions.exp: The leaflet explicitly says unused tablets must be returned to a pharmacy and not kept for future illnesses or given to others, which matches the statement about leftovers. The full course is required even after symptoms improve, a missed dose is skipped rather than doubled, and nothing in the excerpt mentions taking the medicine with food.

questions.stem:
"In a large Spanish trial, volunteers at high cardiovascular risk were assigned by lottery to either a Mediterranean-style diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil and nuts, or to a control diet advised only to limit fat. Over about five years, the Mediterranean groups suffered roughly 30% fewer heart attacks, strokes and deaths from cardiovascular causes than the control group. The benefit appeared without meaningful weight loss and without a rise in calorie intake. The researchers note that the diet as a whole was tested, not any single ingredient, and that participants lived in a Mediterranean country where these foods are familiar and affordable."

From a newspaper report on nutrition research

Indicate which of the following statements is not correct:
options: Assignment to the Mediterranean or the control diet in the trial was random.
Major cardiovascular events were about 30% lower in the Mediterranean groups.
The trial demonstrated the protective effect of extra-virgin olive oil alone.
The benefit did not depend on the participants losing weight.
The researchers evaluated a whole dietary pattern rather than one ingredient.
questions.exp: The passage states that the diet as a whole was tested and not any single ingredient, so the claim that olive oil alone was shown to be protective is the incorrect one. The other statements restate the lottery assignment, the 30% reduction in events, the absence of weight-loss dependence and the whole-pattern evaluation.

questions.stem:
"With the telescope I have detected four small stars that have escaped the notice of every astronomer before me. They attend a certain planet, arranged in a straight line with it, and their distances from the planet change: at times one hides behind the planet or passes in front of it, and they complete their circuits in unequal periods, the nearest the fastest."

Adapted from Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (1610)

What did the author observe?
options: Comets passing close to the Sun
Spots on the surface of the Sun
Fixed stars that never change position
questions.exp: The objects follow a planet, pass behind and in front of it, and circuit it at different speeds like attendants, which identifies them as the four large moons of Jupiter observed by Galileo. Fixed stars do not orbit a planet, comets orbit the Sun, and neither sunspots nor rings match bodies that repeatedly disappear behind a planet in a straight line with it.
questions.topic: Reading · history of science source (Galileo's telescope)

questions.stem:
"An antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria but spares any cells that already carry resistance genes, for example a gene encoding an enzyme that destroys the drug. The surviving cells multiply, and resistance genes can also pass between bacteria on small circles of DNA. In environments where antibiotics are used often, such as hospitals, resistant strains therefore make up a growing share of the bacterial population over time."

From a microbiology textbook

Only one of the following statements is coherent with the excerpt:
options: Bacteria deliberately mutate when an antibiotic is present so that they can survive it.
Antibiotics create resistance genes inside susceptible bacteria.
Resistance genes can never move from one bacterium to another.
Frequent use of antibiotics favours the spread of resistant strains.
Susceptible and resistant cells are killed by an antibiotic to the same degree.
questions.exp: Because the drug spares cells that already carry resistance genes while killing susceptible ones, frequent antibiotic use selects for resistant strains, which then multiply and share genes, so the selection statement is the coherent one. Deliberate mutation and direct creation of genes are misreadings of selection, the passage says genes pass between bacteria on circles of DNA, and by definition susceptible cells are killed more than resistant ones.

questions.stem:
Consider this statement: All squares are rectangles.
Which of the following statements is deducible from the given statement?
options: If a figure is not a rectangle, then it is not a square.
Every four-sided figure is a rectangle.
Squares and rectangles share no geometric properties.
questions.exp: The contrapositive of a universal statement follows with certainty: a figure outside the class of rectangles cannot be inside the subclass of squares. That all rectangles are squares is the invalid converse, and although some rectangles are indeed not squares in ordinary geometry, that fact is not deducible from the given statement alone, which makes it the trap here.

questions.stem:
From the given statements:
If it rains this afternoon, the tennis match will be moved indoors.
If the match is moved indoors, it will start at 2 pm.
The match did not start at 2 pm.
Which conclusion can be deduced?
options: The match was moved indoors but started at a different time.
It did not rain this afternoon.
questions.exp: No 2 pm start means, by modus tollens on the second statement, that the match was not moved indoors, and not being moved indoors in turn means, by modus tollens on the first statement, that it did not rain. Claims about lateness, cancellation or a delayed indoor start add information the premises do not contain.

questions.stem: Amara, Bruno and Chiara live on three different floors of a small building, one person per floor. Bruno lives on the third floor, Amara lives directly above Bruno, and Chiara lives directly above Amara. On which floor does Chiara live?
questions.exp: Bruno is fixed on the third floor, Amara directly above him is on the fourth, and Chiara directly above Amara is on the fifth. The other floors either duplicate Bruno's or place Chiara below her constraints.

questions.stem: Three students, Sara, Tom and Leo, each study exactly one foreign language among French, German and Spanish. Sara studies neither French nor German, and Leo studies German. Which of the following is correct?
questions.exp: Sara excluding French and German leaves her Spanish, and Leo already takes German, so the only language left for Tom is French. Each other option gives Tom or Sara a language already assigned or explicitly excluded.

questions.stem: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of an analogue clock at exactly 9:30?
questions.exp: At 9:30 the minute hand points at the 6, that is 180° round from the 12, while the hour hand has drifted halfway between the 9 and the 10, at 9.5 × 30° = 285°; the difference is 105°. The 90° option freezes the hour hand exactly on the 9 and ignores its half-hour drift.

questions.stem: The small amount of ATP that glycolysis itself produces is formed by:
options: chemiosmosis at the inner mitochondrial membrane.
direct transfer of a phosphate group from a phosphorylated intermediate to ADP.
hydrolysis of the NADH produced in the pathway.
questions.exp: Glycolysis makes its ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation: phosphorylated intermediates such as 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate hand a phosphate group directly to ADP. Chemiosmosis and the electron transport chain belong to oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondrion, and the conversion of pyruvate yields no ATP.

questions.stem: The reaction that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA before entry into the Krebs cycle takes place in:
questions.exp: Pyruvate is first transported into the mitochondrial matrix, where the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidises and decarboxylates it to acetyl-CoA. Glycolysis, which made the pyruvate, happens in the cytosol, and the inner membrane is the site of the electron transport chain.

questions.stem: During the complete oxidation of one glucose molecule to CO₂ and water, carbon dioxide is released during:
options: the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.exp: Of the six CO₂ produced per glucose, two are released by the two link reactions and four by the two turns of the Krebs cycle. Glycolysis produces no carbon dioxide at all, and oxidative phosphorylation transfers electrons to oxygen without releasing carbon.

questions.stem: A substance makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons while leaving the electron transport complexes untouched. The most direct consequences are that:
options: electron transport stops while ATP synthesis continues.
electron transport and ATP synthesis both stop.
ATP synthesis increases while electron transport slows.
the proton gradient grows and ATP synthesis accelerates.
electron transport accelerates while ATP synthesis falls.
questions.exp: A proton leak discharges the gradient that restrains the chain, so electron flow speeds up, but the same lost gradient removes the driving force for ATP synthase, so ATP production drops; this is exactly how uncouplers behave. Stopping both processes would require poisoning the complexes themselves, which the substance does not do.

questions.stem: In the mitochondrial respiratory chain, electrons are carried from complex III to complex IV by:
questions.exp: Cytochrome c is the small soluble protein that ferries electrons between complexes III and IV. Ubiquinone delivers electrons to complex III from complexes I and II, oxygen only accepts electrons at complex IV, and ATP synthase is powered by protons rather than carrying electrons.

questions.stem: In haemoglobin, each oxygen molecule binds to:
options: the iron ion at the centre of a heme group.
a terminal amino group of a globin chain.
a hydrophobic pocket between two subunits.
the membrane of the red blood cell.
a molecule of bicarbonate inside the cell.
questions.exp: Each of the four subunits carries a heme whose iron ion binds one O₂ molecule reversibly; the terminal amino groups are instead where CO₂ attaches, and the red cell membrane holds no oxygen-binding site. This separation of sites is part of why the two gases can be carried by the same molecule without directly competing.

questions.stem: The largest fraction of the carbon dioxide carried in venous blood is transported:
options: bound to the iron atoms of haemoglobin.
as carbamino compounds on plasma proteins.
as bicarbonate ions in the plasma.
inside the organelles of red blood cells.
questions.exp: About 70% of metabolic CO₂ is converted by carbonic anhydrase inside red cells to bicarbonate, which then exchanges into the plasma; smaller amounts dissolve or travel bound to haemoglobin and plasma proteins. CO₂ does not compete for the heme iron, which is oxygen's site, and mature red blood cells have no organelles.

questions.stem: Compared with fast-twitch fibres, slow-twitch (type I) muscle fibres:
options: contain more mitochondria and are more resistant to fatigue.
contain fewer mitochondria and fatigue rapidly.
rely mainly on anaerobic glycolysis for their ATP.
contract more rapidly but for shorter periods.
questions.exp: Slow-twitch fibres are endurance fibres, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin and powered by oxidative metabolism, so they keep contracting for long periods without fatigue. The paler fast-twitch fibres are the ones that depend on glycolysis and tire quickly.

questions.stem: The thin layer of cells lining the inner surface of the heart chambers and of all blood vessels is called the:
questions.exp: The endothelium is the simple squamous epithelium that lines the entire cardiovascular tree. Mesothelium lines the body cavities, perichondrium and periosteum wrap cartilage and bone, and a collagen sheath is extracellular connective tissue rather than a cellular lining.

questions.stem: The activity of an enzyme rises with temperature up to an optimum and then falls steeply at higher temperatures because the enzyme:
options: switches to catalysing a different reaction.
begins to denature, losing its functional three-dimensional shape.
starts to synthesise an inhibitor of itself.
is broken down into its component fatty acids.
questions.exp: Above the optimum temperature, added thermal energy breaks the weak interactions that hold the enzyme's active conformation, and denaturation collapses the active site. The fall is a property of the enzyme rather than of substrate supply, and enzymes are proteins, so they degrade to amino acids, not fatty acids.

questions.stem: Inhibition by a non-competitive inhibitor differs from competitive inhibition in that it:
options: is reversed completely by adding excess substrate.
affects only the apparent affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.
involves the inhibitor binding at the active site.
lowers the maximum rate of the reaction and is not overcome by excess substrate.
disappears when the reaction mixture is cooled.
questions.exp: A non-competitive inhibitor binds away from the active site and takes enzyme molecules out of action, so the maximum rate falls no matter how much substrate is added. Complete reversal by substrate and a change only in apparent affinity describe competitive inhibition instead.

questions.stem: Between meals, bile is stored and concentrated in the:
questions.exp: The liver produces bile continuously, but between meals it is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder, which contracts to release bile into the duodenum when fat arrives. The pancreas supplies digestive enzymes and bicarbonate, not bile.

questions.stem: Soon after a meal rich in carbohydrates, the liver responds to the prevailing hormonal signal by:
options: converting glucose into glycogen for storage.
breaking glycogen down into free glucose.
increasing the loss of glucose in the bile.
questions.exp: Rising blood glucose after the meal triggers insulin, which promotes hepatic glycogenesis, the polymerisation of glucose into glycogen. Glycogen breakdown is the fasting response driven by glucagon, whose secretion falls after a carbohydrate meal, and glucose holds no nitrogen to be made into urea.

questions.stem: The osmotic gradient of the renal medulla, which allows the production of concentrated urine, is created mainly by active salt transport in the:
questions.exp: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle pumps sodium and chloride into the medullary tissue while remaining impermeable to water, building the osmotic gradient that the collecting duct later exploits to reabsorb water under ADH. The glomerulus filters blood, the proximal tubule reabsorbs glucose and nutrients, and the distal tubule fine-tunes ion balance.
questions.topic: Bio · kidney (loop of Henle and medullary gradient)

questions.stem: The cells whose beating cilia sweep mucus and trapped dust upward out of the airways are:
questions.exp: The airway lining contains ciliated cells whose coordinated beating moves the overlying mucus blanket up to the pharynx, where it is swallowed. Goblet cells secrete that mucus, type I alveolar cells form the gas-exchange surface, macrophages patrol the alveoli, and chondrocytes build the cartilage rings.

questions.stem: Iodine is required in the human diet mainly for the synthesis of:
questions.exp: The thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) are the body's only iodine-containing hormones, and prolonged iodine deficiency enlarges the thyroid into a goitre. Insulin, adrenaline, antidiuretic hormone and cortisol contain no iodine.

questions.stem: The α-helix and the β-pleated sheet are features of which level of protein structure?
questions.exp: Secondary structure is the regular local folding of the polypeptide backbone, stabilised by hydrogen bonds, and the α-helix and β-sheet are its two classic forms. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, tertiary is the complete fold of one chain, and quaternary is the assembly of multiple chains.

questions.stem: According to the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane, the proteins of the membrane:
options: can drift laterally within the lipid bilayer.
are each fixed rigidly in a single position.
occur only on the outer surface of the membrane.
form a solid continuous coat over the bilayer.
questions.exp: The bilayer is a two-dimensional fluid in which integral proteins migrate sideways, as demonstrated when proteins from two fused cells mix across the hybrid membrane. Carbohydrates decorate only parts of the membrane's outer face, and nothing in the model makes it a solid coat.

questions.stem: The digestive enzymes inside lysosomes have an optimum pH of about:
questions.exp: Lysosomal hydrolases work best near pH 5, matching the proton pumps that acidify the organelle's interior; the acidic lumen also protects the cell, because enzymes escaping into the cytosol at about pH 7.2 lose most of their activity. A pH near 2 belongs to the stomach.

questions.stem: Catalase, the enzyme that decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, is concentrated in which organelle?
questions.exp: Peroxisomes carry out oxidation reactions that generate hydrogen peroxide and contain abundant catalase to destroy this toxic product. Lysosomes digest macromolecules at acidic pH, mitochondria synthesise ATP, and the Golgi and nucleolus process proteins and ribosomal subunits.

questions.stem: For a cross between two heterozygotes, Aa × Aa, the expected ratio of genotypes AA : Aa : aa among the offspring is:
questions.exp: The Punnett square of Aa × Aa produces one AA, two Aa and one aa, so the genotypes appear in the ratio 1:2:1. The 3:1 ratio is the phenotypic one, because AA and Aa share the same appearance, and 9:3:3:1 belongs to a dihybrid cross.

questions.stem: Red-green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele carried on the X chromosome. A man with colour blindness and a woman with normal vision whose father was colour blind have children. Which statement is correct?
options: All of the daughters will be colour blind.
All of the sons will be colour blind.
The daughters cannot have received the allele from their father.
On average, half of the sons and half of the daughters will be colour blind.
All of the children will have normal vision.
questions.exp: The woman must be a carrier, because her colour-blind father passed his only X chromosome to her; crossing an affected man with a carrier woman gives, in equal proportions, carrier daughters, colour-blind daughters, colour-blind sons and normal sons. Every daughter does receive the colour-blind allele from her father, but half of the daughters also receive a normal allele from the mother and so are only carriers.

questions.stem: During elongation of translation, the new peptide bond forms between the growing polypeptide chain and:
options: the amino acid carried by the tRNA that has just entered the A site.
the codon currently being read in the mRNA.
the tRNA about to leave through the E site.
the ribosomal RNA of the small subunit.
the anticodon of the following tRNA.
questions.exp: The ribosome transfers the growing chain from the tRNA in the P site onto the amino acid of the tRNA that has just arrived at the A site, extending the polypeptide by one residue. Codons and anticodons carry the genetic information but no amino acid, and the tRNA leaving the E site departs without its cargo.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.001 mol/dm³ aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide, a strong base? (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C)
questions.exp: Sodium hydroxide dissociates completely, so [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³, pOH = 3, and pH = 14 − 3 = 11. The value 3.0 is the pOH mistakenly read as pH, and 13.0 would correspond to a 0.1 mol/dm³ solution.
questions.topic: Chem · pH of a strong base

questions.stem: At 25 °C, pure water has Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ and pH 7. At 80 °C, Kw rises to 4.0 × 10⁻¹³. In pure water at 80 °C, the concentration of H⁺ and the nature of the water are:
options: [H⁺] = 2.0 × 10⁻¹³ mol/dm³ and the water is basic.
[H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol/dm³ and the water is neutral.
[H⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻¹³ mol/dm³ and the water is acidic.
[H⁺] = 6.3 × 10⁻⁷ mol/dm³ and the water is neutral.
[H⁺] = 6.3 × 10⁻⁷ mol/dm³ and the water is acidic.
questions.exp: In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = √Kw, so at 80 °C the concentration is √(4.0 × 10⁻¹³) ≈ 6.3 × 10⁻⁷ mol/dm³, giving a pH of about 6.2. The water is still neutral, because neutrality means equal concentrations of the two ions and not a pH of exactly 7; equating [H⁺] with Kw itself, or keeping the 25 °C value, produces the wrong concentrations.
questions.topic: Chem · Kw and neutrality at higher temperature

questions.stem: Which of the following substances has a giant covalent (network covalent) structure?
questions.exp: Diamond is an endless lattice of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds, the defining giant covalent structure. Sodium chloride is ionic, copper is metallic, and ice and methane are molecular, discrete molecules held to each other only by weaker forces.

questions.stem: Water (M = 18 g/mol) boils at 100 °C, while methane (M = 16 g/mol) boils at −162 °C. The main reason for the much higher boiling point of water is:
options: covalent bonds linking the atoms of different molecules.
the larger number of covalent bonds inside each water molecule.
the slightly greater molecular mass of water.
questions.exp: Each water molecule can donate and accept hydrogen bonds through its O–H bonds and lone pairs, and this strong intermolecular attraction demands much energy to break, hence the high boiling point. The molecules themselves are not linked covalently or ionically, and a 2 g/mol mass difference cannot explain a 260 degree gap.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of phosphorus in H₃PO₄?
questions.exp: Hydrogen contributes 3 × (+1) and oxygen 4 × (−2), so phosphorus must be +5 for the sum over the neutral molecule to be zero. The value +3 belongs to phosphorous acid, H₃PO₃, with one oxygen fewer, and the higher values cannot be balanced by this formula.
questions.topic: Chem · oxidation numbers (phosphorus in phosphoric acid)

questions.stem: In the reaction 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃, which species is the oxidising agent?
options: Fe²⁺, because it combines with chlorine.
Fe³⁺, because it is the product of the reaction.
Cl⁻, because it carries a negative charge.
Cl₂, because it accepts electrons from the iron and is itself reduced.
Neither species, because no electrons are transferred.
questions.exp: Iron climbs from +2 to +3, meaning it loses electrons, and chlorine drops from 0 to −1, meaning it gains them; the electron acceptor, Cl₂, is by definition the oxidising agent. Fe²⁺, which donates the electrons, is the reducing agent, and charges or product status alone do not define the role.

questions.stem: How many open-chain alcohols have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O?
questions.exp: The four alcohol isomers are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol, from the straight chain with the hydroxyl at either end or the middle, and the branched chain with the hydroxyl on the end carbon or the central one.
questions.topic: Chem · organic chemistry (structural isomers of butanol)

questions.stem: The bond formed between the amino group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of another is called:
questions.exp: Joining two amino acids by a condensation reaction links the amino group of one to the carboxyl group of the other and releases a molecule of water, forming a peptide bond. Glycosidic bonds join sugar units, ester bonds join glycerol to fatty acids, and phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides.

questions.stem: What amount, in moles, is present in 8.8 g of carbon dioxide? (M(CO₂) = 44 g/mol)
questions.exp: Dividing mass by molar mass, 8.8 g ÷ 44 g/mol = 0.2 mol. The value 0.44 comes from dividing by 20 instead of 44, and 2.0 from inverting the ratio and multiplying.

questions.stem: A sample of gas occupies 4.0 dm³ at 300 K and 100 kPa. If the sample is heated to 600 K at constant pressure, its volume becomes:
questions.exp: At constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature, so doubling the temperature from 300 K to 600 K doubles the volume from 4.0 dm³ to 8.0 dm³. The 2.0 dm³ option wrongly halves the volume on heating, which reverses the relationship.

questions.stem: Going down group 1 of the periodic table, from lithium towards francium, the reactivity of the metals with water:
options: decreases, because the atoms become smaller.
remains constant, because every group 1 metal has one outer electron.
decreases, because the outer electron is held more tightly.
increases, because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is lost more easily.
questions.exp: Down the group each new shell places the single outer electron further from the same nuclear charge felt through similar shielding, so it is lost more readily and the metal reacts more violently with water. The atoms grow larger, not smaller, and the count of outer electrons alone does not fix the reactivity.

questions.stem: The electron configuration of a neutral atom of sulfur (Z = 16) is:
questions.exp: Filling in order, 2 + 2 + 6 electrons complete the first two shells and 3s², leaving 16 − 12 = 4 electrons in 3p, giving 3s²3p⁴. The second option is argon's configuration with 18 electrons, and the others place electrons in ways that violate the sublevel order or the total count.

questions.stem: For the equilibrium 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the equilibrium constant K is given by:
questions.exp: The equilibrium constant is product concentrations divided by reactant concentrations, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, so numerator [SO₃]² and denominator [SO₂]²[O₂]. The first option drops the exponent on SO₂, and the fourth inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: When the temperature of a reaction mixture is raised, the rate of the reaction increases. Which property of the reaction remains unchanged?
options: The fraction of molecular collisions energetic enough to react.
The activation energy of the reaction.
The frequency of collisions between reactant molecules.
The number of reactant molecules able to react.
The rate at which products form.
questions.exp: The activation energy is fixed by the reaction's own pathway and does not depend on temperature; what changes is the distribution of molecular energies, so a larger fraction of collisions exceeds that unchanged barrier, collisions occur more often and the rate rises. The rate itself is exactly what increases, so it cannot be the unchanged property.

questions.stem: The compound formed between the aluminium ion, Al³⁺, and the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, has the formula:
questions.exp: Two Al³⁺ cations give +6 and three SO₄²⁻ anions give −6, so charge balance requires Al₂(SO₄)₃, with the polyatomic ion in parentheses because it appears more than once. The other formulas leave a net charge and so cannot represent a neutral compound.

questions.stem: Solve the inequality 1 − 2x ≥ 5.
questions.exp: Rearranging gives −2x ≥ 4, and dividing by −2 reverses the inequality, so x ≤ −2. Forgetting the reversal gives x ≥ −2, and stopping one step early gives the options involving 2 without the minus sign change.

questions.stem: The set of real solutions of the inequality (x − 2)² ≥ 0 is:
options: the set of all real numbers
questions.exp: A squared real number is never negative, so (x − 2)² is at least zero for every real x, and the whole real line satisfies the inequality, with equality only at x = 2. Choosing only x = 2 confuses the solution of the strict equality with that of the inequality.

questions.stem: In a class of 40 students, 25 study French, 18 study German and 9 study both languages. How many students study neither language?
questions.exp: By inclusion-exclusion, the number studying at least one language is 25 + 18 − 9 = 34, so the 40 − 34 = 6 remaining students study neither. The 15 option counts only the students not studying French, forgetting those who study German alone, and 34 stops at the union without subtracting it from the class.

questions.stem: If 3x + 2y = 12 and y = 3, then x equals:
questions.exp: Substituting y = 3 gives 3x + 6 = 12, so 3x = 6 and x = 2. The value 3 merely copies the given y and 4 comes from dividing 12 by 3 before subtracting the 6.

questions.stem: The expression x² − 16 can be factorised as:
questions.exp: This is the difference of squares, x² − 4² = (x − 4)(x + 4). The perfect-square options wrongly keep an x term that is not present, and x(x − 16) expands to x² − 16x.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has legs of 6 cm and 8 cm. Its perimeter is:
questions.exp: The hypotenuse is √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 cm by Pythagoras' theorem, so the perimeter is 6 + 8 + 10 = 24 cm. The 14 cm option adds only the two legs and forgets the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, one angle is 30° and the hypotenuse has length 10 cm. The side opposite the 30° angle has length:
questions.exp: The sine of 30° is exactly 1/2, so the opposite side is 10 × 1/2 = 5 cm. The 5√3 cm value belongs to the side adjacent to the 30° angle, since cos 30° = √3/2.

questions.stem: The velocity-time graph of a cyclist is a horizontal line at 6 m/s for the whole interval from t = 0 to t = 10 s. The distance covered in this interval is:
questions.exp: Constant velocity means distance is speed times time, 6 × 10 = 60 m, the area of the rectangle under the graph. The 30 m option wrongly halves the speed as if starting from rest and accelerating, and 600 m multiplies by 100 instead of 10.

questions.stem: When a 12 V battery is connected across a lamp, a current of 0.5 A flows. The resistance of the lamp is:
questions.exp: Ohm's law gives R = V/I = 12/0.5 = 24 Ω. The 6 Ω option multiplies instead of dividing, and 48 Ω double-counts the voltage.

questions.stem: A 60 W lamp is left switched on for 2 hours. The electrical energy it consumes is:
questions.exp: Energy is power multiplied by time, and 60 W is 0.06 kW, so 0.06 kW × 2 h = 0.12 kWh. Each neighbouring option misplaces the decimal point by one factor of ten.

questions.stem: A box slides across a level floor at constant velocity. The resultant (net) force acting on the box is:
options: equal to the friction force and directed forwards.
directed forwards and larger than the friction force.
equal to the weight of the box.
questions.exp: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by Newton's first law the forces balance and the net force is zero: the forward push equals the backward friction. The force equal to friction but pointing forwards is the pushing force, not the resultant, and the weight is balanced by the normal reaction.

questions.stem: An astronaut weighs about one sixth as much standing on the Moon as standing on Earth because:
options: the astronaut's body contains less matter on the Moon.
the Moon's smaller gravitational acceleration acts on the astronaut's unchanged mass.
the Moon has no atmosphere to push up on the astronaut.
part of the astronaut's weight is still carried by the distant Earth.
weight cannot be measured where there is no water or air.
questions.exp: Weight is mass multiplied by the local gravitational acceleration, and the Moon's smaller mass and radius give about one sixth of Earth's surface acceleration, so the same mass weighs one sixth as much. The quantity of matter in the astronaut does not change between locations, and the atmosphere plays no part in defining weight.

questions.stem: An object weighs 50 N in air. When it is fully submerged in water, its apparent weight is 40 N. The buoyant force exerted by the water on the object is:
questions.exp: The water pushes up with a force equal to the loss of apparent weight, 50 − 40 = 10 N, which by Archimedes' principle equals the weight of the displaced water. The 40 N and 50 N options confuse the apparent or true weight with the buoyant force itself.
